extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students (practitioners in patent infringement litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules governing the defenses to patent infringement (origin/inventive act, inventorship, priority, statutory class, and novelty/prior use). Focused on what proof each side must introduce and what inferences the court/jury may draw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence (inventive act / reduction to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent itself is prima facie evidence that the alleged invention is the result of an inventive act and that the invention had been made when the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduction of the patent satisfies the plaintiff's initial burden; the defendant must then overcome the presumptions arising therefrom. The court will take judicial notice and may declare a patent invalid if want of inventive skill is apparent on the face of the patent. Reduction to practice may be shown by the specifications and drawings, or by actual use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence (patentee performed inventive act / inventorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent is prima facie evidence that the patentee or his assignor performed the inventive act resulting in the alleged invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overthrow this evidence the defendant must prove by conclusive testimony that some specific person other than the alleged inventor conceived the invention, that the alleged inventor obtained knowledge of it, and procured a patent falsely claiming it. Evidence such as admissions, declarations of others uncontradicted by the patentee, company records, or proof of immediate adoption after learning can be used to show nonperformance by the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence (priority / first inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent is prima facie evidence that the patentee is the first inventor of the described improvements; the burden is on the defendant to show prior invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defendant must show conception before the patentee's and either reduction to practice or reasonable diligence in reducing it to practice. The date of the patentee's conception is assumed to be the patent date (or filing date if the application is referred to). The defendant must prove prior invention beyond reasonable doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence (novelty / patentability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff's patent furnishes prima facie evidence that the invention described and claimed is patentable (novel and within statutory classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being in evidence, the burden rests on the defendant to prove want of novelty or nonpatentability. The weight of the patent as evidence may be enhanced by PTO scrutiny, extensions, or successful interference results (though those matters have separate evidentiary rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of burdens of proof and presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of a patent satisfies certain plaintiff burdens and creates presumptions which the defendant must overcome; the specific burdens depend on the defense raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inventive skill, performance, priority, novelty, and statutory-class issues the patent shifts initial proof to the plaintiff; the defendant bears the burden to rebut the patent's prima facie case (often 'beyond a reasonable doubt' for priority/novelty). Where doubt exists on the whole testimony, the patentee is entitled to a verdict on issues like inventorship/performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive skill is a question of evidence (First Defence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether inventive skill was involved in the production of the alleged invention is a question for the jury in view of the state of the art at the date of the inventive act and of the result attained, unless lack of inventive skill is apparent on the face of the patent (then the court may declare invalid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant may prove lack of inventive skill by competent lay or expert witnesses. If jury entertains reasonable doubt as to inventive skill, the prima facie evidence of the patent must prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence showing lack of inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible proof that an alleged invention lacks inventive skill includes showing it was suggested by existing appliances, merely a rearrangement or variation in constructive details, an idea only of a force/function/effect (not means), or never reduced to a tangible/practical embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant may show the inventor did not discover a new capability, new susceptibility, or new mode of connecting force/object, or that the idea never passed beyond mental conception. Such evidence is admissible from lay or expert witnesses familiar with the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence showing inventive skill (plaintiff rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff may rebut attacks on inventive skill by demonstrating the idea was an 'idea of means' and that it was reduced to practice before application, and by presenting expert testimony, evidence of great utility, and general public acceptance as indicia of inventive genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superior working, great utility, and wide acceptance can support an inference that inventive skill was necessary. Re-issues that agree with originals may be conclusive evidence of invention as described in the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice: forms of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice may be shown by the patent's specifications and drawings, by actual use, or by contemporaneous models/descriptions showing a practical, available form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual use proves reduction to practice; specifications and drawings can suffice when they disclose a practical embodiment. Diligence in perfecting and bringing to use is relevant for priority disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof required to show patentee did not perform the inventive act
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebut the presumption that the patentee performed the inventive act, the defendant must prove by conclusive testimony that (1) some specific person other than the alleged inventor conceived the invention, (2) the alleged inventor obtained knowledge of that invention, and (3) the alleged inventor procured a patent falsely claiming it as his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence admissible includes testimony of the true inventor, contemporaneous descriptions/models, admissions by the patentee, declarations of others uncontradicted by the patentee, company records, and proof of immediate adoption after learning. No proof of actual bad faith is necessary; piracy in fact suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority (Third Defence): conception, diligence, and reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: On a priority defense the defendant must show the rival inventor conceived the invention earlier than the patentee and either reduced it to practice first or exercised reasonable diligence toward reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date of conception by the plaintiff's inventor is assumed to be the patent date (or filing date if referred). The rival's conception can be proved by testimony, contemporaneous models or descriptions; reduction to practice by witnesses who knew of production in a form available for immediate practical use. Diligence is measured against the inventor's health, means, and command of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference proceedings and prior administrative findings
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision in interference proceedings is admissible and entitled to grave consideration but is not conclusive on a jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adverse Patent Office decision places the burden accordingly in later litigation, but court decisions and PTO findings carry weight without removing the defendant's evidentiary burden in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory-class test (Fourth Defence): within protected classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The court must determine whether the patented invention is embraced within one of the statutory classes of patentable subject matter (art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, design, or improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a jury question generally, but the court may take judicial notice and direct a verdict for the defendant if on the face of the patent it is evident the invention is not within protected classes. The necessary attributes of each class are matters of law; evidence should be confined to showing conformity of the invention (as construed by the court) with those legal definitions, and typically consists of opinions from persons skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination vs simple aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an alleged invention purports to be a combination, the defense may attempt to prove its elements do not cooperate to produce a unitary result and therefore that it is only a simple aggregation (not patentable as a combination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must be confined to the conformity of the invention to the legal definition of a combination; distinctions and resemblances are typically shown by experts skilled in detecting such features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty defense structure (Fifth Defence): three-prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty issue embraces three questions: (1) prior use in this country making the invention accessible to the public; (2) prior patent; (3) prior printed publication placed within reach of the public before the patentee's date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affirmative answer to any of these negates legal novelty and therefore the patent's validity. The patent answers these questions in the negative and thus shifts to the defendant the burden of proving the affirmative beyond a reasonable doubt. Evidence types include prior uses, prior patents (domestic and foreign as probative), and printed publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use: accessibility and proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior use requires that the art or article had been used in such a manner in the country as to render it accessible to the public at the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of prior use may be by testimony of witnesses who knew of its production or use, contemporaneous models or descriptions; actual use proves reduction to practice. The effect of public accessibility rather than mere private use is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and sources of patent-evidence and foreign patents/publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patents (e.g., British) and prior foreign acts are prima facie evidence of novelty/value but have limitations; the weight of a patent as evidence is influenced by PTO scrutiny, re-issue, extension, and other administrative history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A British patent proves itself but only as prima facie evidence; a foreign inventor cannot always carry the date of invention back by acts done in a foreign country. The defendant still bears the burden of showing lack of novelty despite such foreign documents being admissible.
